title: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems

fields.label: Label
fields.value: No hidden regularity beyond repetition and nesting in rule-30-like systems

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: There is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems with complex behavior such as rule 30; beyond systems with obvious regularities like repetition and nesting, most systems are universal and computationally equivalent.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 12: The Principle of Computational Equivalence

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: I have gradually come to the conclusion that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of systems, and that instead what the Principle of Computational Equivalence suggests is correct

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 12, “The Principle of Computational Equivalence”; section “Explaining the Phenomenon of Complexity” (from p. 735), p. 735. Scope: simple programs with non-repetitive, non-nested behavior, such as rule 30

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch12-11: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.30

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Public enumerations permit meaningful searches and counterexamples in chosen families. No feasible analysis can confirm the universal negative or infer computational equivalence merely from failure to detect structure.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For explicitly sampled simple-program families, search for algebraic invariants, compression, prediction shortcuts, and universality proofs beyond repetition and nesting. Discovery of a broad exploitable invariant would refute a restricted version; repeated failure would not prove absence.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A 'large class' and 'hidden regularity' have no unique definitions.

Universality does not imply absence of all useful regularities.

Absence of hidden regularity is not finitely verifiable.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.15
operationalizability: 0.3
data existence: 0.55
discriminating power: 0.25
analysis feasibility: 0.15

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: For rule 30, arbitrarily long samples can be generated and subjected to published statistical and algebraic tests, which is enough to hunt specific hidden regularities. A found closed form would refute the claim for that system. No such test, and no universality proof, establishes the general statement that there is no hidden regularity in any large class of complex systems.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix a class, such as rule 30 and a list of similar rules, and a catalog of candidate regularities stricter than periodicity and nesting, including algebraic closures, conserved quantities, and standard randomness tests. Discovery of such a regularity in a large subclass refutes the claim for that class; passing the catalog supports only the absence of those particular regularities.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Tests can detect only regularities they are designed to find; passing them does not prove that no regularity exists.

Any large class is undefined until the class is listed.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.4
data existence: 0.6
operationalizability: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.35
